About.title: About
About.metaDescription: Dialectio is a map of how words sound in the world's languages and in Ukrainian dialects. How to read the map and where the data comes from.
About.intro: Dialectio shows on a map how the same concept is written, pronounced and sounds in the world's languages and in the dialects of Ukrainian. It is a popular-science project: it aims to spark curiosity, not to replace a dictionary.
About.numbers: On the map now: {concepts} concepts, {languages} languages, {dialects} dialects, {words} words and {recordings} recordings by real speakers.
About.how1: Type a word in any language and pick a suggestion: countries that have a translation light up and the words appear on the map.
About.how2: Zoom in on Ukraine or its neighbours: from a certain zoom level, words are shown per region instead of per country. Dialect words are purple.
About.how3: Click a country or region to keep only the languages and dialects spoken there in the panel.
About.how4: IPA in square brackets is the pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet. The ▶ button plays a recording; TTS marks a synthetic voice.
About.how5: The ≈ mark means an unverified word: a draft, a Wikidata concept label or a machine translation. Under such a word you can answer “Do people say it like this?”: once enough people say yes, it gets the 👥 mark (confirmed by speakers), while ⚠ marks a disputed word. An editor makes the final check.
About.dialects: Dialects follow the classic scheme: three dialect groups (Northern, South-Western, South-Eastern) and 15 dialects. Dialect areas are approximated by regions, which is a simplification: real dialect borders do not follow administrative ones. Lemko and Nadsian are also shown in Poland and Slovakia.
About.help: Do you know how this word is said in your village or town? Click “Know how it’s said where you live?” in the word panel, type the word and, if you like, record it. Contributions appear on the site after an editor reviews them.
About.feedback: Spotted a mistake? Tell us on <link>GitHub</link>.

Sources.metaDescription: Where Dialectio gets its words, pronunciations, audio and maps, and under which licenses.
Sources.intro: Every word and recording on the site keeps its source. The license and author of each recording are shown in the tooltip of its ▶ button.

Privacy.title: Privacy policy
Privacy.metaDescription: What data Dialectio collects and how it is used.
Privacy.intro: You can use Dialectio without an account. We use no tracking cookies and share no data with ad networks.
Privacy.contrib: We store what you enter in the form: the word, the language or dialect, the place and a voice recording (optional), and that your account sent it. After review, the name of your account and the place may be shown next to the word. By sending a contribution you allow Dialectio to publish it.
Privacy.ip: To fight spam, the server temporarily remembers how many contributions, votes and reports came from an IP address (in the last hour or day). This is not written to the database.
Privacy.browser: The site remembers in your browser (localStorage) the dialect you last picked in the contribution form, your votes, your region and a random id for voting. Apart from the votes, this is not sent to us.
Privacy.third: The basemap is loaded from OpenFreeMap servers and some audio from Wikimedia Commons. These services see your IP address, like any site your browser loads something from. To keep bots out, the sign-up, email and add-a-word forms are checked by Cloudflare Turnstile: it sees your IP address and technical browser data, but sets no advertising cookies.
Privacy.delete: To delete your contribution or voice recording, write to us on <link>GitHub</link> with the word and the dialect.
Privacy.stats: To learn which words people find interesting, we count page views with Umami, running on our own server. It uses no cookies, stores no IP addresses and does not follow you across sites: we only see totals — how often a page was opened, from which country and which site.
Privacy.votesTitle: When you vote or report a mistake
Privacy.votes: We store your vote (yes or no) and the text of a mistake report. So that one browser has one vote per word, your browser creates a random id; the server keeps only its hash, which cannot be turned back into the id. The region, if you gave it, is stored with the vote and helps refine the dialect map.
Privacy.search: When a search finds nothing, we keep the search text and a counter so we can add the word to the dictionary. Nothing about you is stored with it.
Privacy.account: We keep your email address, your name and a hash of your password (the password itself is neither stored nor recoverable from the hash). If you sign in with Google, Google gives us only your (verified) email address and your name; no password is needed then. After signing in, the browser gets a session cookie, used only to keep you signed in. Your votes and control-card answers are linked to the account. You can delete the account in your profile: email, name and sessions go at once, votes stay anonymous. The languages and dialects in your profile and your speaker test results are kept with the account and deleted with it; words you added stay on the site without your name. Emails (confirming your address, a new password, sign-in links) are sent through Brevo (Sendinblue SAS, France): it receives only your address and the email itself.

Dialects.title: Dialects of Ukrainian
Dialects.metaDescription: Three dialect groups and 15 dialects of Ukrainian: where they are spoken and which words they use, with a map, translations and pronunciation.
Dialects.intro: Ukrainian dialects fall into three groups. Pick a dialect to see its area on the map and its words with standard Ukrainian equivalents.

Dialects.otherDialectsIntro: How the same thing is called differently across one language's regions. In German a bread roll is Brötchen, Schrippe, Semmel or Weckle; in Italian a watermelon is anguria, cocomero or melone d'acqua, depending on the region.

DialectInfo.ukr-polissia-west: The West Polissian dialect is spoken in the Polissia of Volyn and Rivne. It has diphthongs and other vowels in place of old o and e (кунь, нуч for кінь, ніч) and old vocabulary shared with Belarusian dialects.
DialectInfo.ukr-polissia-central: The Central Polissian dialect is spoken in northern Zhytomyr and Kyiv regions. Stressed old o and e turn into diphthongs: куонь, нуоч.
DialectInfo.ukr-polissia-east: The East Polissian dialect is spoken in the Chernihiv region and northern Sumy. It has diphthongs like куінь and much in common with neighbouring Russian and Belarusian dialects.
DialectInfo.ukr-volhynian: The Volhynian dialect is spoken in southern Volyn and Rivne and western Zhytomyr. It is transitional between the Polissian and Podillian dialects.
DialectInfo.ukr-podillian: The Podillian dialect is spoken in the Vinnytsia and Khmelnytskyi regions. Known for words like пшінка (maize) and бараболя (potato).
DialectInfo.ukr-dniester: The Dniester dialect is spoken along the Dniester in the Lviv, Ternopil and Ivano-Frankivsk regions. Many loans from Polish and German: ровер (bicycle), шклянка (glass), склеп (shop).
DialectInfo.ukr-nadsian: The Nadsian dialect is spoken along the San river: western Lviv region and Subcarpathia in Poland. It is close to the Dniester and Lemko dialects.
DialectInfo.ukr-boyko: The Boyko dialect is spoken in the mountains of the Lviv and Ivano-Frankivsk regions. Typical words: хижа (house), облак (window), ногавиці (trousers).
DialectInfo.ukr-hutsul: The Hutsul dialect is spoken in the Carpathians: Ivano-Frankivsk, Bukovyna, Transcarpathia and Maramureș in Romania. Known for words like ґазда (master), ватра (fire), полонина (mountain meadow).
DialectInfo.ukr-pokuttia-bukovyna: The Pokuttia-Bukovyna dialect is spoken in Bukovyna (Chernivtsi region and Suceava in Romania) and Pokuttia. Many Romanian loans: патлажан (tomato), папушой (maize).
DialectInfo.ukr-transcarpathian: The Transcarpathian dialect is spoken in Transcarpathia. Many Hungarian and Slovak loans: крумплі (potato), уборка (cucumber), погар (glass).
DialectInfo.ukr-lemko: The Lemko dialect is spoken in Lemkivshchyna: the Polish Carpathians (Lesser Poland, Subcarpathia) and the Prešov region of Slovakia. Written with the letter ы: хыжа, лыжка.
DialectInfo.ukr-middle-dnieper: The Middle Dnieper dialect is spoken in the Kyiv, Cherkasy and Poltava regions. It is the basis of modern standard Ukrainian, so it differs from it the least.
DialectInfo.ukr-slobozhan: The Slobozhan dialect is spoken in the Kharkiv and Sumy regions. Close to the Middle Dnieper dialect, with noticeable Russian influence.
DialectInfo.ukr-steppe: The Steppe dialect is spoken in southern and eastern Ukraine: Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Donetsk. The youngest dialect, formed by settlers from many regions.

Terms.title: Terms of use
Terms.metaDescription: Rules for using Dialectio: data, contributions, liability.
Terms.service: Dialectio is a popular-science site that shows on a map how words sound in different languages and dialects. Some words were collected automatically or are unverified drafts (marked “≈”), so the data may contain mistakes. The site does not replace a dictionary or a scholarly reference.
Terms.content: Every word and recording keeps its source and license (see “Sources”). Wikidata data is CC0, Wiktionary translations are CC BY-SA 4.0 (credit the source and share alike), Wikimedia Commons audio follows each file's license. Dialectio's own data (editors' words, drafts, descriptions, dialects) is protected by copyright; quoting with a link to the site is allowed.
Terms.contributions: By sending a word or a voice recording, you confirm that you have the right to do so and give Dialectio permanent, free permission to use and publish the contribution, including commercially. Contributions appear after review; we may reject, correct the spelling of or delete a contribution.
Terms.conduct: Do not send offensive, false or other people's material, advertising or spam, and do not try to manipulate votes or overload the site. We may restrict access for anyone who breaks these rules.
Terms.liability: The site is provided “as is”, without any guarantee of accuracy or availability. We are not liable for consequences of using the data. Links to other sites lead to resources their owners are responsible for.
Terms.changes: We may update these terms; the date of the last update is shown at the top of the page.

FalseFriends.title: False friends with Ukrainian
FalseFriends.metaDescription: Words in other Slavic languages that sound like Ukrainian words but mean something else: Polish “lis”, Bulgarian “гора”, Russian “неделя”.
FalseFriends.intro: Some words in other languages sound almost like Ukrainian words but mean something quite different. Polish “lis” is a fox, not a forest (Ukrainian “ліс”); Bulgarian “гора” is a forest; Russian “неделя” is a week. Pick a language:

FalseFriends.langIntro: These words ({language}) look or sound like Ukrainian words but mean something else. They were found automatically by sound, so some are chance coincidences.
